misconception: Your tools and data live in silos — Claude can never reach them.

mentorLessons.line: MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. Think of it as a USB-C port for AI: one standard plug, many devices.
A connector links Claude to an app you already use — it can retrieve your data and take actions inside that service. The silos were never sealed; they just lacked a bridge.
Three roles hold every bridge: the host (the AI application), which creates one client per connection, and the server, which provides the context. One dedicated client per server — no shared ropes.

A server offers three gifts: tools (functions the AI can invoke to act), resources (data that provides context), and prompts (reusable templates). Actions, information, and patterns — learn which is which.
A local server runs on your own machine and talks over stdio; a remote server runs elsewhere and talks over streamable HTTP, serving many clients at once. Same protocol, different roads.

Connectors typically use OAuth: you sign in to the service itself and grant specific permissions — no password handed over, and you can revoke it all by disconnecting. Claude never gets more access than you already have.

A custom connector reaches a server no one at Anthropic has verified. Only connect to servers you trust, read the permissions you grant, and disable tools you don't need — a malicious server can smuggle instructions through prompt injection.
Ready-made connectors live in the Connectors Directory; a custom one just needs its remote MCP server URL. Either way, you choose what gets bridged.

Cloud service? Use a remote connector — they work everywhere you use Claude. Local files, a localhost database, OS-level access? That needs a local desktop extension, which only works in Claude Desktop and Claude Code.

questions.prompt: A guildmate scoffs: "Every AI-to-tool hookup is a bespoke one-off integration." What is MCP, actually?
choices: A proprietary Anthropic-only plugin format
A database Claude ships with
An open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems
A programming language for agents
questions.reteach: MCP is an open standard, so any AI application and any tool can speak the same connection language.
hardChoices: An Anthropic SDK for building Claude-only connectors
A REST API specification for calling LLM providers
A marketplace of verified integrations published by Anthropic

questions.prompt: The official docs compare MCP to a piece of everyday hardware. Which one, and why?
choices: A USB-C port — one standardized way to connect many things
A padlock — it keeps data sealed away
A hard drive — it stores your context
A CPU — it does the model's thinking
questions.reteach: MCP is like a USB-C port for AI: one standard connection instead of a custom cable per device.
hardChoices: A universal remote — one device that operates every app for you
A docking station — it hosts all your tools in one place
An HDMI cable — it streams context straight into the model

questions.prompt: You enable a Google Drive connector in Claude. What does that actually make possible?
choices: Claude memorizes your entire Drive permanently
Claude can retrieve your data and take actions in that service during a conversation
Nothing — your files are in a silo Claude can never reach
Google gains access to your Claude chats
questions.reteach: A connector lets Claude access a connected service to retrieve data and take actions — the silo gets a bridge.
hardChoices: Claude gains standing background access to Drive between conversations
Claude syncs a full copy of your Drive into its context window
Claude gets admin rights to manage sharing across your workspace

questions.prompt: What technology do Claude's connectors use under the hood?
choices: Screen scraping of each app
Emailed export files
A custom secret protocol per app
The Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard
questions.reteach: Connectors are built on MCP — an open standard for AI applications to connect to tools and data.
hardChoices: OAuth — the authorization protocol itself carries the data exchange
Anthropic's proprietary Claude Integrations API
Function calling built directly into the model weights

questions.prompt: In MCP terms, when Claude Desktop connects to a GitHub MCP server and a filesystem MCP server, what is Claude Desktop?
choices: An MCP resource
The MCP host, which creates one client per server connection
An MCP server serving two clients
A transport layer
questions.reteach: The AI application is the host; it spins up one dedicated MCP client for each server it connects to.
hardChoices: An MCP client that shares one connection across both servers
The MCP server, since it provides context to the model
The host, which shares a single client between the two servers

questions.prompt: A host is connected to three MCP servers. How many MCP clients does it maintain?
choices: One shared client for all servers
Zero — servers connect directly to the model
Three — a dedicated client per server
It depends on how many tools each server has
questions.reteach: Each MCP client maintains a dedicated connection to exactly one server, so three servers means three clients.
hardChoices: One — the host itself acts as the single client
One pooled client connection, reused across the three servers in turn
Two — local servers can share a client; remote ones cannot

questions.prompt: An MCP server for a database exposes a "run query" function and, separately, the database schema as readable context. In MCP terms, those are…
choices: Both tools
A tool and a resource, respectively
A prompt and a tool, respectively
Both resources
questions.reteach: Tools are executable functions the AI can invoke; resources are data sources that provide context.
hardChoices: A resource and a tool, respectively
Two tools — anything a server exposes counts as a tool
A tool and a prompt, respectively

questions.prompt: Which MCP server primitive is a reusable template for structuring interactions, like a few-shot example set?
choices: A resource
A tool
A notification
A prompt
questions.reteach: Prompts are the third server primitive: reusable templates that help structure interactions with the model.
hardChoices: A resource, since it's stored data the model reads
A tool the client invokes to format its messages
A sampling request sent from the server to the client

questions.prompt: Before calling any tool on a freshly connected server, what does an MCP client do first?
choices: Discover what's available with a tools/list request
Guess tool names from the server's URL
Download the server's source code
Nothing — tool lists are hardcoded into the model
questions.reteach: Clients discover primitives dynamically — they list available tools before calling them, so listings can change over time.
hardChoices: Read the server's resources to infer which tools exist
Fetch the tool schemas from the Connectors Directory listing
Complete an OAuth grant authorizing each tool individually

questions.prompt: One MCP server runs on your own machine over the stdio transport; another runs on a company's platform over streamable HTTP. What are these commonly called?
choices: Primary and backup servers
Fast and slow servers
A local server and a remote server
A client and a host
questions.reteach: Stdio-transport servers on your machine are 'local'; streamable-HTTP servers running elsewhere are 'remote'.
hardChoices: A desktop extension and a connector — the transport names the product
A stdio client and an HTTP client
A private server and a public server

questions.prompt: Which kind of MCP server typically serves many clients at once?
choices: A local stdio server
Neither — every server is single-client
Both equally, always
A remote streamable-HTTP server
questions.reteach: Local stdio servers typically serve one client; remote streamable-HTTP servers typically serve many.
hardChoices: A local stdio server, since stdio streams support many readers
The MCP host, which fans connections out to many clients
Any server, once it is published in the Connectors Directory

questions.prompt: You add a connector and it asks you to sign in to the service itself and approve specific permissions. Why is this OAuth flow the standard approach?
choices: It grants scoped access without ever giving Claude your password
It's faster than typing a password into Claude
It gives Claude permanent irrevocable access
It lets Claude bypass the service's own access rules
questions.reteach: OAuth lets you sign in at the service and grant specific permissions — your password is never shared, and you can revoke access by disconnecting.
hardChoices: It hands Claude an encrypted copy of your credentials to reuse
It certifies that Anthropic has reviewed the server's code
It raises Claude's access above your own account's permissions

questions.prompt: A teammate fears a connector will let Claude read files in their company drive that they themselves can't open. What's true?
choices: Correct — connectors bypass source-system permissions
Correct, but only on weekends
Wrong — Claude's access is limited to content you can view in the source system
Wrong — Claude can see everything but won't mention it
questions.reteach: Connector access rides on your own permissions — Claude can't see anything in the source system that you can't.
hardChoices: Wrong — Claude only reads files you attach, never the drive itself
Right — remote servers run with the service's admin credentials
Wrong — Anthropic reviews each file before Claude can open it

questions.prompt: You find a random unofficial MCP server URL on a forum and consider adding it as a custom connector. What's the real risk?
choices: Custom connectors are always safe because Anthropic reviews each one
Nothing — servers can only send data, never influence behavior
The URL might load slowly
It's unverified by Anthropic, and a malicious server can use prompt injection to trigger unintended actions
questions.reteach: Custom connectors reach servers Anthropic hasn't verified — only connect to trusted ones, since malicious servers can attempt prompt injection.
hardChoices: None, as long as the server supports OAuth sign-in
Only that its tools won't appear in the Connectors Directory
None — remote servers can't be risky; only local ones touch your machine

questions.prompt: You've connected a custom connector that exposes a dozen tools, but you only need two. Good practice?
choices: Disable the tools you don't need and review what each permission grants
Enable everything — more tools is always safer
Delete your account to be safe
Never look at the permissions screen; it's just legal boilerplate
questions.reteach: Reduce your surface area: review permissions carefully and disable tools you don't actually need.
hardChoices: Keep all tools enabled — the model only calls the ones you mention
Switch it to a local server, which needs no permission review
Trust the OAuth grant — a signed-in server can't misuse its tools

questions.prompt: You want to stop a connected service's access entirely. What's the sanctioned way?
choices: Ask Claude to promise not to use it
Disconnect the connector — that revokes the permissions you granted
There is no way; connections are permanent
Change your Claude display name
questions.reteach: You can revoke a connector's permissions at any time by disconnecting it.
hardChoices: Request its removal from the Connectors Directory
Change your password at the service so Claude's stored copy expires
Uninstall Claude Desktop — every connector lives on your machine

questions.prompt: Your team wants to hook Claude up to a service it already uses, plus one in-house tool with its own remote MCP server. Where does each connection come from?
choices: Both must be built from scratch in code
Neither is possible — external tools stay siloed
Browse the directory of available connectors for the first; add the in-house one as a custom connector via its remote MCP server URL
Email Anthropic support to install both
questions.reteach: Ready-made connectors are in the directory; anything with a remote MCP server can be added as a custom connector by URL.
hardChoices: Both come from the directory — custom servers must be listed there first
Install both as local desktop extensions on each teammate's machine
Use the directory for the first; point Claude at the in-house REST API docs URL

questions.prompt: You need Claude to work with a cloud project tracker from your phone, and separately with files on your laptop's disk. Which connector types fit?
choices: Local for both — local is always more powerful
Remote for the cloud tool (works everywhere you use Claude); a local desktop extension for the laptop files (Claude Desktop / Claude Code only)
Remote for both — remote servers can read any laptop's disk
Neither — Claude cannot reach tools or files at all
questions.reteach: Remote connectors are the default and work across surfaces; local desktop extensions handle on-machine access but only in Claude Desktop and Claude Code.
hardChoices: A desktop extension for the tracker; a remote connector for the laptop files
Remote for both — streamable HTTP lets the server reach your local disk
Local for both — desktop extensions sync across every surface you use
